newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stoiber continues battle against soft euro - paper.
newsitem.headline: Stoiber continues battle against soft euro - paper.

text.p: Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber has pushed ahead his crusade against a soft euro by threatening to vote against the common currency unless strict deficit goals are met, Germany's Bild newspaper said on Friday.

Stoiber, a member of the hardline conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), has drawn attention this week by promising to put up fierce resistance to any attempt to soften the euro eligibility criteria.

The CSU party, including party-leader and German finance minister Theo Waigel, has said a nation's deficit ratio may be no greater than 3.0 percent to Gross Domestic Product in 1997 to qualify for currency union.

The newspaper said Stoiber had decided he would vote against the introduction of the euro in Germany's upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, if all Maastricht Treaty criteria were not met exactly.

"I am not waging an anti-euro discussion. I am not waging an anti-chancellor (Helmut Kohl) discussion but rather a discussion for a permanently stable euro that will be and will remain as strong as the mark," Bild quoted Stoiber as saying.
Stoiber's vocal demands are the latest in a string of problems to plague the Bonn government in its preparations for currency union, scheduled to begin in January 1999.

And as Germany struggles to squeeze its budget deficit into the Maastricht criterion, French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Thursday said the French public deficit in 1997 would exceed three percent of gross domestic product.
